sentences.text: Diplocynodon was an extinct eusuchian crocodilian that lived in Europe, resembling the modern caiman with a bony armor of osteoderms covering its neck, back, belly, and tail.
Some species of Diplocynodon may have reached lengths of 3 meters, while others were likely smaller than 1 meter.
The largest known species, D. hantoniensis, measured 5.9 meters (19.5 feet) in length.
Most articulated Diplocynodon specimens from the Messel Pit and Geiseltal contain gastroliths, which are stones swallowed to aid digestion.
The genus Diplocynodon was first described by Pomel in 1847.
The type species of the genus Diplocynodon is Diplocynodon ratelii.
Well-preserved specimens of Diplocynodon have been found in the Messel Pit and the Geiseltal lignite deposit in Germany.
Martin and colleagues reported in 2026 that fossil material of Diplocynodon was found in Oligocene strata in central Turkey, marking one of the easternmost known records of the genus.
Diplocynodon species are almost exclusively found in freshwater environments.
Researchers believe the various species of Diplocynodon were opportunistic aquatic predators.
Skull shape analysis suggests Diplocynodon was a small generalist carnivore that shared resources with the larger Asiatosuchus.
Isotopic analysis of enamel from Late Oligocene specimens indicates Diplocynodon primarily fed on aquatic vertebrates.
Osteohistological analysis suggests D. hantoniensis had a growth pattern similar to the modern American alligator, with determinate, seasonally-controlled growth.
CT scans of D. tormis have reconstructed internal snout and brain structures, providing insights into its sensory and cognitive capabilities.
Diplocynodon is considered one of the most basal members of the superfamily Alligatoroidea.
Diplocynodon belongs to the alligatoroid group of reptiles known as Alligatoroidea.
Fossils of Diplocynodon date from the Paleocene to the Middle Miocene.
